variable {S F : Type*} [BasicModalLogicalConnective F] [DecidableEq F] [System F S] {𝓢 : S} [System.GL 𝓢]
informal_statement: For every natural number \( n \), there exists a prime number \( p \) such that \( p > n \). This implies that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
informal_proof:
Let \( n \) be an arbitrary natural number. Consider the number \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), which is at least 2 since factorial grows rapidly and adding 1 ensures the result is greater than 1. This number must have at least one prime factor \( p \) because every integer greater than 1 has prime factors.

Assume, for contradiction, that \( p \leq n \). However, since \( p \) divides \( (n + 1)! \) (by definition of factorial) and also divides \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), it must divide the difference between these two numbers, which is 1. The only divisor of 1 is 1 itself, but \( p \) is a prime number, which by definition is at least 2. This contradiction implies that our assumption \( p \leq n \) is false. Therefore, \( p > n \).

Since \( n \) was arbitrary, this reasoning holds for all natural numbers \( n \). Thus, there are infinitely many prime numbers.

informal_proof:
